utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are present. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Bourgon, that's about it. Yes. Mr. Obradovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your testimony. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you to slow down your natural rate of speech and to wait to make a pause before you start answering my question. You can look at the cursor moving on the screen in front of you. That should be an indication as to when you can start speaking. So first I would like us to eliminate some of the confusion engendered by the transcript yesterday and the Prosecution also indicated that there was some confusion. So my first question to you will be, did you ever become a commander of the 283rd Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the 327th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the one in Derventa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never became a commander. Twice in a period of six months I stood in for the commander in addition to being a commander of the 327th Armoured Brigade, which was my usual duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now that we are on this topic of standing in for the commander, could you please tell us how did you come in to stand in for the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to my establishment, my post was the Chief of Staff. At the same time, I was the deputy commander. That's what it says in the establishment. When Colonel Suljic was the commander, Zitro when he retired, then this post was temporarily vacant. And now, I don't know why the commander of the corps, of the 17th corps, did not issue a decision but issued an order for me to stand in. And that is why I stood in for the commander in addition to my usual duties, and I had all the powers and duties vested in the brigade commander. I also went into the higher pay grade, and I also got the commander's supplement as was stipulated. And also I had all the powers that inherent in this establishment post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In 1993, so we are talking now about 1992, but let us move on to 1993. What I want to know is whether in 1993 and 1994 until the 1st of September you still had the status or rather the command duty of the Chief of Staff of this brigade in Derventa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the order to stand in expired, appropriate changes were made. A new commander was appointed, and I was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And it is from this post that you come to the Main Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to the Main Staff, I would like us to clarify one more issue. Your promotions that you had in the course of war and in its aftermath, in 1994 you were promoted to lieutenant-colonel [as interpreted]. Could you please tell me as your career progressed did you receive any other promotions in terms of military ranks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was next promoted to the rank of colonel, that was in June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: There is a mistake in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 3, line 13, it says that in 1994 you were promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you were promoted to that rank earlier; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So after you received the rank of lieutenant-colonel, when were you promoted to the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I received the rank of colonel in June of 1995. And I was promoted to general after the war, that was in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And finally, as regards your status, you are retired now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that you joined the Main Staff in 1994 on the 1st of September to the administration for operations and training?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, to put it quite simply, this administration what did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration for operations and training was part of the staff, the Main Staff of the VRS, and it had three elements: The operations department, the training department, and the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You told me that the chief of the administration was Colonel Miletic at that time. Could you please tell me what duty did you take on when you joined the administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty was the chief of the operations department. And if you are referring to functions --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Could you please tell me what -- who was the chief of the training department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel Krsto Djeric; he was the chief of the training department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me the third element, the third department in the operations and training administration? What about it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations centre is the third element of the administration, in accordance with the establishment, had to have at its head the chief of the training operations centre, two shift leaders, and one operator. But because of shortage of personnel, that element was not set up in this manner but what was set up was the operations duty element through the operations duty officer of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you are talking about the operations duty element, does that involve the operations duty officers at all levels of the command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations duty officers existed at all levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Including in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, what were the staffing levels in the operations and training administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the establishment that was in force at that time, the operations and training administration had to have 18 officers. That was the officer complement. And our staff included four officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did the staffing levels remain the same up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who was the fourth officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the operations department, it was Lieutenant Dragan Micanovic. He was a cartographer; he had a degree in land surveying and topography.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So Krsto Djeric, who was the chief of the training department, you and Dragan Micanovic, had Colonel Miletic as a -- you all had him as your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Miletic was my superior and the superior of Colonel Djeric, and I was the immediate superior of Lieutenant Micanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you in what sector or -- I withdraw that question. What was the structure in terms of organisation of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Main Staff had at its head the commander, the cabinet, and the department for civil affairs that was linked with the cabinet. It had five sectors and, also, administration, separate administrations. The sectors were Sector for Staff Affairs, Sector for Morale, Education and Legal Affairs, the Logistics Sector, the Sector for Organisation, Mobilization and Personnel, Sector for Security and Intelligence, the Administration for Airforce and Air Defence, and the Administration For Planning, Development, and Finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: All those sectors that you listed, were they the command, in fact?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what sector did the administration for operations and training belong to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations and training administration was an integral part of the Sector for Staff Affairs, that also included the organs for branches of the army, the information technology organ, the office, and the typing pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the Staff Affairs Sector?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the establishment, it was also the deputy commander, and it was General Manojlo Milovanovic. And the chiefs of the other sectors in the command --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. The chiefs of the other sectors in the command, were they also assistants to the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in immediate contact with the commander and they were members of the corps command and assistants to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we then --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well the only thing is that the chief of the sector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Because this is becoming frustrating to me. Frustrating to me, at least, I can imagine how more frustrating to the interpreters. You need to slow down both of you. And I am not making any distinction between the witness and counsel this time. You need to allow, first and foremost, what Mr. Petrusic is asking you to be translated to us. You will know if it's translated completely when the cursor on your screen stops completely. Like this, you are creating havoc. Let's proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, we really have to abide by the instructions that we have just received, and there is a mistake -- or rather it was impossible to interpret one part. So let us go back to the personnel of the commands of the Main Staff. You spoke about the corps command and the chiefs of the sectors or assistants to the commander. So could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the sector chiefs and the chiefs of the two independent administrations were at the same time assistants to the commander. And they were, in fact, the core [Realtime transcript read in error, "corps"] command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction to the transcript: It's C-O-R-E command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 8, line 3, the witness did not say "corps command" but "core" as in C-O-R-E command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please confirm that this is, indeed, so?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document 5D1039 up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you have this document in the folder in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D1039.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who issued this document, what command, and who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see from the heading that this is the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. The document was logged on the 22nd of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the last page of this document, that's page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the signature block of this document, does it say deputy commander Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version that's the previous page, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So General Milovanovic, was he in the Main Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the 22nd of December [as interpreted] [Realtime transcript read in error, "November"] -- or, rather, October [Realtime transcript read in error, "okay"] I'm sorry. This was a document that was drafted on the day or maybe a day or two before General Milovanovic left with a group of officers from the Main Staff to the western front in order to establish a forward command post pursuant to the decision of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction for the transcript. At page 9, line 2, it should read not "November" but "October."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, what was the reason why General Milovanovic with this group of officers went to the western front?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, the defence was disrupted, and there was a break through by the HVO units in the direction of Kupres; and the 5th Corps of the BH army also carried out the breakthrough in the Bihac area in the direction of Krupa and further down to Ripca. And after a brief assessment, the commander made this decision to send his deputy to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This order bears the number 03/4, I am not going to read any further, but could you please tell me what sector -- or, rather, what administration was the originator of the memo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This designation, numerical designation 03/4, it's the designation of the trainings and operations administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in administrative terms what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that this document was drafted in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last page of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be the fourth paragraph in the Serbian version, and in the English version it's the paragraph marked (F).

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, for your reference it's also listed under (F) but this sentence begins with: "In coordination with the IBK ..." have you been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please read to yourself this paragraph and then please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the task that was assigned to the Drina Corps where in coordination with its neighbouring units to the right, that would the Eastern Bosnia Corps, it should mount a decisive defence of the Zvornik area, and also the axes leading from Olovo and Kladanj towards Sokolac, Hans Pijesak, and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And does the Chief of Staff in this order provide any other information to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a conditionality here that if the UNPROFOR forces withdraw from the enclaves that the Drina Corps forces should be -- should stand ready to liberate Srebrenica and Zepa using their own forces and in a coordinated action with the Herzegovina Corps, they should also liberate the Gorazde enclave. And it says here that the previous operation, MAC-3, should continue according to the original plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And finally, please look at the paragraph number 7. And I would like you to comment on the first sentence, which begins with the words: "Based on this order ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, what is ordered here is that the corps command should plan their own operations with the exception of the corps -- corps that actually carry out operations in accordance to the current plan. And they are ordered to draft the secret commanding of troops documents. And they should stick with those plans, abide by them. And as far as communications are concerned, the communications are to be maintained in accordance with the existing plans, with strict adherence to the cryptographic -- encryption documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to page 1 of this document where it says quite clearly who the addressees are, who this order is issued to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind that you had an opportunity to look at this order and to inspect it in some detail, and what tasks are assigned here, to the corps -- corps, since it is issued to the commands of all the corps, what kind of combat documents -- how would you classify this document in terms of combat documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer this question, yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get just a little foundation. This is an operations document. At the time I believe he was operations, and his -- if we are going to get his opinion on it, I think that's fine. But if he remembers it, was involved in drafting it? I think it would be a lot more helpful for his testimony if we knew that, or if he's just reading it today for the first time and telling us what he thinks it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if I could actually force or suggest to Mr. Petrusic to do what you propose. I think you can do that yourself later on. On the other hand, I can barely understand what he means by: "How would you classify this document in terms of combat documents?" I don't know what you mean. Perhaps if you did go a little bit deeper it would make it more understandable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in principle, what kind of combat documents are there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directives, commands, orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, in brief terms we will be dealing with that later at greater length, but what are directives?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directives are used by the highest level of the command, strategic and operative levels of the command. And they differ from combat orders in that long-term tasks are issued in terms of the objectives that are set. So we are talking about a longer term here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In this document, do we have tasks that are longer-term tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the formulations for the tasks assigned to the Drina Corps and to other corps, the duration is longer than usual, and that is why this kind of falls into the gap between the two kinds of documents. It says "combat orders" here but the way in which the tasks are phrased is more reminiscent of a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So be that as it may, you say that General Milovanovic left with a group of his officers, either on that day or a day or two later, after this order was issued. So could you tell us which officers accompanied him to the western front?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the late General Jovo Maric, who was the chief of the administration for air force and air defence; the chief of the artillery branch, Colonel Dragisa Masal. I can't recall who the others were. I think that -- I know that an element from the communications regiment went there to set up communications at a forward command post. The officers from the military schools command were also involved. They were sent to that area -- to that place, and I think -- or, rather, I am sure that the assistant for morale from the East Bosnia Corps, Colonel Slobodan Jelacic also went.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And you remained in the Main Staff, did you not? And tell me whether you stayed there until the very end of the war, did you remain in the same position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remained chief of the operations department. However, at the request issued by the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, General Miletic, who was colonel at the time, referred me to Bijeljina; and from Bijeljina where I spent the night, I travelled together with Colonel Jelacic to the forward post of the Main Staff which had been organised in the village called Jasenica in the hinder land of the Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At that forward command post --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At that forward command post, General Milovanovic was posted there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at that forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in Jasenica until the end of December 1994. At that time, the four-month agreement on cease-fire was signed with the Muslim side. And then we moved to Drvar. That is where General Milovanovic planned combat operations to return the positions that had been lost in the Livno Polje. The line was from Capazrlje [phoen] to Celebic, that's the line that I am talking about. And he left Colonel Masal in Jasenica. And that position was then named forward command post 2. 2 as in figure 2. And then sometime in January, Colonel Masal had been summoned to urgently go back and visit his family for some reasons, I don't know what reasons those were. And General Milovanovic asked me to replace him in Jasenica. Colonel Masal returned on the 26th of January; and on the 27th I broke my leg. And I was transferred to Brana Luka, to the clinical hospital there, and I never returned to the previous position after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And after that sick leave, where did you return?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka on the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In Crna Rijeka, while you were there and were -- while the chief of the Main Staff, General Milovanovic was there, and while General Mladic was also there, the commander of the Main Staff, as well as the other assistants and the chief of administration for operations and training, General Miletic. Who was in charge of the coordination of the organs of the command while you were all there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was testimony Chief of Staff who was in charge of the coordination of the organs of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And who would be in charge of that coordination if General Milovanovic was absent as the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the commander because coordination is a function of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Since on the 17th of July you returned from sick leave, i.e., you were in the Main Staff at that time, do you know whether General Miletic in July 1995, while there was fighting around Zepa, coordinated the work of the organs of the command?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. You need to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know whether General Miletic in July 1995 indicated --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Off mike. Off mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was it that coordinated the work of the command in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander. He coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of General Miletic ever being in charge of the coordination of the work of the command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic coordinated the work of the staff in the administration, in the staff between the departments and when he was standing in for General Miletic [as interpreted]. And as for the coordination of the work of the organs of the Main Staff, it was not something that he could do, especially in view of the fact that the assistant commanders by their rank, function, and position would be higher ranking than him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is an important section, and it doesn't make sense on the transcript. I think "standing in for General Milovanovic" is what is supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know how best to go about this, but what we have is, "General Miletic coordinated the work of the staff in the administration" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter misspoke and apologies. It was General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Thank you, so we can proceed then. What are we waiting for?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, who was the one who was the officer -- strike that. Would General Mladic, when he left the command post, appoint an officer or a person that would be in charge of the coordination of the work of the command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff, if his deputy is there, has no reason to do that. But, if both the -- if the Chief of Staff is also present -- absent because he has to leave, he will then appoint a person who would stand in for him during his short absence from the command post and who would be in charge of his duties and coordination. In other words, he has to appoint one of his assistants to stand in for him during his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce document number 5D1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the command of the Drina Corps on the 14th of June, 1995, signed by commander -- corps commander, Major-General Milenko Zivanovic. The document bears the title: "Order to enable normal functioning of commanding by commanders when the commander is away from the corps KM," standing for command post. You've had an occasion to see this document, so I would kindly ask you to comment upon it for us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic obviously has some bad experience with order and discipline at the command post. And that's why he issued this order to regulate the situation. When he was absent from the command post, the Chief of Staff had to remain in the command post; although, this would be a customary matter regulated by the rules and regulations. And at all levels, the principle of interchangeability should have been taken into account; but here he reminds everybody of something that is a well-known fact that the Chief of Staff should be there while he is gone. But he also leaves an open possibility for the Chief of Staff to leave the command post, to appoint a person that would stand in for him at the command post until the moment when either the commander or the Chief of Staff are able to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What would be your comment of paragraph 3 of this order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that this speaks about the work at the command post. Under bullet point 3, he orders the communications squad to provide the commander with certain types of communication in the mobile communications centre, because he does not actually give anybody the authority to takeover the command over the corps. He just organises work at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We've had an occasion to hear people talking about a commander's deputies to be able to act only in the spirit of the commander's decisions. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputies at all levels, Chief of Staffs who also stand in for the commander or are deputies to the commander, rather, have the right to order units, but in the spirit of the general command or decision that had previously been issued by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now see document number P410. In the English version, I would kindly ask for page number 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Look at the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7. And page 9 in the English version, as I've already said. In the Serbian version, it would be page number 7, Article 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have page 4 on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version it is page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In the English version, is it page 9 or not? Because to me they don't seem to correspond. I may be wrong, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. President. That's -- that's article or, rather, page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we see in English is page 9, and page 9 is what the transcript said you said. Initially you said page 7, but then you said page 9. Okay. This is better. All right. Now they correspond. So for the record page 8 in English, page 10 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, this is the regulations on the authorities of the commander in the ground forces in peacetime, and this is the chapter dealing with the organs of the staff. The subsection is, "Chief of Staff," and this regulates the obligations in Article 11. What I am interested in is this Article 11, paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please move to the next page in the English version. Could we please look at paragraph 9. In Serbian version, it's again at the next page. Well, finally we are getting there. Just a moment, please. In the Serbian version, could you please move to the next page. And in the English version, too, please. Well, finally, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at the last sentence after Article 13 where it says: "The Chief of Staff in his absence shall have the Chief of Staff for operations in training standing in for him."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I believe misspoke in his question or perhaps it was left out; but the regulations he's referring to are the core regulations of the JNA from 1990; and so I think it's incumbent upon a foundational question for this witness to say whether or not they are applicable to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what do you have to say to that Mr. Petrusic? I think Mr. McCloskey is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, before providing an answer to my question, could you please tell us what regulations, what laws applied to the procedures in the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Republika Srpska army, the procedures were adopted from the legislation that was in force in the former JNA for the most part. We, in the Main Staff, did not have the regulation on the authority. And these regulations, the provisions for the corps, could not apply to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment. So you mean to tell us, and you told us, that you followed the regulations from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The -- this regulation deals with the authorities of -- within the corps -- corps of the ground forces in peacetime. It was issued by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of the armed forces of the Socialist Republic of the Former Yugoslavia. It was issued in 1990. So the commands and installations of the army of Republika Srpska, and in particular the corps, did they operate in accordance with this regulation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps did, because the 1st Krajina Corps was the successor of the former 5th JNA corps, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps succeeded or had the same headquarters and also had some of the officers from the 4th Corps of the JNA. So that they applied the same documents that had been drafted by their predecessor corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So my question to you is in the last sentence of this Article 13 of this regulation, it is stipulated that when the Chief of Staff is absent, he shall have the chief of the operations of training organ standing in for him. This provision of this regulation, did it apply in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been applied there, because in the establishment where the corps was set up, the assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training, has a designation of the deputy Chief of Staff. That's always put in parenthesis after the original post. And in the establishment that applied to the Main Staff Command of the VRS, in this establishment, the chief of the operations and training administration did not have the deputy chief of Main Staff as a designation next to this function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D431 up on our screens. So here we have a document that is entitled: "Establishment Number 111900, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska." In the Serbian version, we are looking at page 2. And in the English version that would be page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Under 10, number 10, you can see the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on the previous decision or, rather, your view that you expressed to us previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, could we have just some foundation from what this piece of paper is, where it came from, does he recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially to us who don't read the language, because on the B/C/S version there seems to be a title which could be indicative. But the English one that I am looking at myself doesn't have a title. So -- yes, Mr. Petrusic, if you could go through this quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I want to say that this document was obtained from the secretariat for the Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal of the Republika Srpska at the request of the Defence; and it has been in evidence for some months now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As regards the objection, I would like to ask you this, General, having seen the first page of the document, do you recognise this document? In the course of the your military career did you ever come across this document, do you know what this document is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the establishment organising the Main Staff of the VRS; and it is on the basis of the establishment that I exercise some rights, enjoyed some rights, based on the elements that were contained in this establishment just like any other member of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what did the legislator [as interpreted] envisage in this establishment in terms of the organisation of the staff or, rather, the operations and training administration, and your operations department? But please wait for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it may be a translation issue, but it says, "what did the legislator, determine ..." I don't think we have a legislator involved here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer that question myself. And still I don't have a clue what document we are looking at. What is -- can someone translate the title of the first two lines, three lines of this document, please? I mean, in English we have don't have -- in English we have part of it without the title. I think we need to see the first page. Yes, that's better. Yes okay. "Summary of duties and units of establishment elements army of Republika Srpska Main Staff." All right. Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When I said "legislator," I primarily meant the legal nature of this document. This is a legal document, but at the insistence of the Prosecutor, I will now ask you, General, whether this is an overview of the various duties, unit by unit, and by establishment elements of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army as is indicated in heading of this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at the first entry here it says, "Duties," that's the first column. And then it says -- you have the codes here. And then there is a column with four sub-columns, and that's formation elements, the number of formation elements, military specialty, rank, and pay grade. In other columns you have listed the weapons and vehicles that belonged to either the individual or the establishment unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What I am interested in is the first column, "Duties," and let us go back to the staff now. Under number 10, we can see that we have the Chief of Staff at the same time the deputy commander. I would now like you to comment on item 12 where it says, "Operations and training administration." That's a heading?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here the chief. There is only establishment post, the military specialities 31099, which means that this person appointed to this post has to have the -- a degree from the National Defence School. As for the rank, this person can be either a colonel or a general, and the pay grade is six.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In accordance with this establishment, is it envisaged that the chief of the operations and training administration is at the same time the deputy of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can see that the Chief of Staff is, in fact, the deputy commander; and there where you see the chief of the operations and training administration, there is no such indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next title is, "The Department for Operations." That is your department.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Move up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please move the document up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next title is "Department for Operations." Is that your department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Under 14 you will see, which is on the next page, it's -- it says: "Chief (at the same time deputy chief) of the administration for the operations and training." Would you please comment upon this entry as well as?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said at the beginning that I was appointed to that establishment post, that I was also the deputy chief of administration, and this also provides a different establishment, elements, the rank, the pay grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After you left for Jasenica, i.e., to the western part of the front line, did you have somebody who remained in your position in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position was not vacant. I was still what it says here in this establishment scheme. And I was dealing with some issues at the forward command post of the Main Staff. I was attending to some tasks there. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you were physically not present at the staff of the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka and that was all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the performance of your duties, did you come across with a regular combat reports, i.e., with regular combat reporting? Tell us just briefly, because we will dwell upon the details a bit later.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was part of my regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who were the combat reports sent to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat reporting is carried out at all levels, from the lowest along the line of subordination, from brigades to the corps, from the corps to the Main Staff, from the Main Staff to the Supreme Commander. In that we resorted to a variant in order to achieve better and higher quality reporting towards the corps, towards the airforce and the entire Aircraft Defence and the military school centre. We sent our unified reports intended for the Supreme Commander to them as well, as well as to the forward command post of the Main Staff that were operational at the specific moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you left to the forward command post in the western part of the front, and when you were there, did you receive combat reports from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the signatory of these combat reports was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the regular procedure, it was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that part of the front line in the forward command post in question, from Manojlo Milovanovic was there from the end of October, wasn't he? Do you know whose signatures did combat reports bear?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was an encrypted communication in the bottom left part of each telegram, there was a so-called block signature featuring the Chief of General Staff, Colonel General Manojlo Milovanovic, but we doubt his actual signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now kindly ask the Court to produce document P51. Let's please look at the first page and the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Having done that tell us, please, whether this would be one of the combat reports that we've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I drafted this one myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. We will come back to this a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe this is a good time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. We will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you said that this was a regular combat report and that the block signature standing in for the Chief of Staff is General Radivoje Miletic, and the date is the 24th of July, 1995. In the English version, this block signature is on the last page. Tell me, please, you were in the Main Staff at that time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know if General Miletic was indeed standing in for the Chief of Staff Manojlo Milovanovic during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not standing in for the Chief of Staff. In order for somebody to stand in for somebody whose establishment post was vacant or if that person was temporarily prevented from discharging those duties, there should be proceeded by an order. And I know that General Miletic did not have an authority to stand in for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also said on page 27 that when General Milovanovic was in his command post, and you -- in the forward command post where you also were for a while, in the autumn of 1994, that combat reports with -- arrived at the IKM featuring the block signature of the Chief of Staff Manojlo Milovanovic. How long did this practice go on for? How long did regular combat reports arrive featuring the block signature of General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December 1994, when we moved to Drvar, every morning, just like in corps commands, a report would await on General Milovanovic's table at the IKM. While we were sipping our morning coffee, he would read the report. General Maric was there, I was there, and then I will have to be a bit vulgar now when I quote him, Why is this Miletic fucking up with me? We looked at him in wonderment, and then he says, How am I supposed to be sending reports to myself? Because the block signature contained his name; and he, himself, was reading that report being General Milovanovic at the IKM. What happened after that, whether there were some oral orders issued, I don't know, but after that a new practice was introduced in which says, "Standing in for the Chief of Staff, Major-General Radivoje Miletic." Although, in my view, it should have been more appropriate if it said, "Upon the approval of the Chief of Staff," rather than "Standing in for." This would have been better in my view, and it would have been more congruent with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you going to say something else, did I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce the following Exhibit, PD1194 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you will see the document on the screen in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is 5D1194. In the English version, we are looking for page 24, and in the Serbian version we are looking for page 43. Can we please look at the page starting with number 65 in the Serbian version, and that is page 43. Thank you very much. This is excellent. The English version is okay. We have what we need. Please scroll up the English version, scroll up a little bit more. We want to see -- yes, perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, this document is the rule on official correspondence and office operations in the Army of Yugoslavia dating back to 1994. Under chapter 10, Article 65, it says, "Signing of Documents." Let's dwell upon the first three paragraphs and let's comment upon them. Let us hear your comment. Could you please read the paragraphs to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objecting to relevance, unless there can be a foundation that this VJ document had applicability in July 1995. So just a question or two of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start with the last -- with the latter of the two points made by Mr. McCloskey. Was this still applicable in July of 1995? Perhaps you can direct the question straight away to the witness, if you can -- if you wish, Mr. Petrusic. Because then the question of relevance or otherwise will fall in naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you've heard first the suggestion and then the question by the Presiding Judge. Could you please tell us whether these regulations where you applied in the army of Republika Srpska in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did apply this regulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you still contest the relevance at this point? No, of course not. Thank you, let's proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce 5D1198. We would like to eliminate any relevance of the objection that we've just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, looking at this document issued by the Chief of Staff of the administration for training and operations, Colonel Radivoje Miletic, on the 12th of March 1995. Would you say that this document refers precisely to the rules of office operation and business that we discussed a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an accompanying letter, which accompanied 21 pieces of that instruction for office operations and business. And the subordinated units who are the addressees of this instruction had to confirm receipt by signing a -- this accompanying document, and the instruction was sent to them in order to allow them to apply it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to 5D1194 now, please, page 43 in the Serbian version and page 24 in the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question to you was to comment upon this Rule 65.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 65 in this instruction on office operations, speaks about the signing of the documents created by the unit command or an institution. It says that the documents should be signed by the officer, the unit command, or the chiefs of the relevant institutions. It also allows for the possibility that the -- establishment deputy or person standing in for the person in charge is allowed to sign such documents. In the second paragraph, it allows the commanding officer of an institution the right to transfer his obligation and duty to sign a document on to another person in the command or institution who is the person to whom he has transferred part of his duties. The bolded part specifically emphasizes that the authorised person cannot transfer that authority on to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we go back to the establishment that -- of the Main Staff that you have had an occasion to see, and if you establish a relationship between the chief of the Main Staff, Manojlo Milovanovic, and the chief of the administration for trainings and operations, General Miletic, the first paragraph of this document which speaks about the establishment deputy and persons standing in for a commander, would this first paragraph be a -- be applicable to that situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By establishment, a chief of administration is neither a deputy nor a person standing in for somebody, but the Chief of Staff has the right to transfer his duties and obligations to the most senior officer and particularly the authority to sign documents. However, and I repeat in the document, in the daily report that we've just seen, this was not the best wording. It is a bit awkward where it says here, "Standing in for."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can feel the stress and the tension in the interpreter's voice. Please slow down. They have already a very, very difficult job. Amongst all the people that work here in the Tribunal, the interpreters have a terrible job sitting in a small cubical and having to cope with what we present them with. So please, try to understand and make their lives a little bit easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Since you were with General Milovanovic at the forward command post, would you say that General Milovanovic was in a position or whether he, indeed, performed his regular duties as the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This could be applied to the Chief of Staff and the commander at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, while he was in the western front, could General Milovanovic have contacts with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had daily contacts with him via protected connection using KZU63.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And as for the other members of the staff or the command, did he have the same means of communications that he could use?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at 5D1278.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is an intercept dated 18 April 1995. The conversation took place at 9.46 in the morning. Could you please read it, and then we will welcome your comments upon it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read this aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No, you can read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here the chief of administration for operations and training, briefs the Chief of Staff. And here it says that he's probably in Sanski Most, that there are no particular problems on the lines, and that the forces of the Drina, and East Bosnian Corps, in the territory of Mount Majevica. And I quote, for the most part did not do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Based on this document -- or, rather, could General Milovanovic have a full insight into the developments of the staff as you are looking at this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the regular combat reports that present the situation at 1700 hours everyday, and individual exchanges via communication means, the superior officers did learn about the developments in the areas of responsibility of the respective corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at 5D1222. This is a document from the Herzegovina Corps command, dated the 1st of August, 1995. It is sent to the Main Staff of the VRS, "Attention General Mladic." It is sent by the commander of the Herzegovina Corps, Radovan Grubac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know where General Mladic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here, "The Main Staff of the VRS, 2nd Krajina Corps, attention General Mladic." So he was at the command post of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was General Milovanovic also in the area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in those parts, but whether he was actually there at the time I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So my question to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are overlapping again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question then is whether the corps commanders were able to send reports directly to the commander or the Chief of Staff even when they were not actually in the command post in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have a case where the commander of the Herzegovina Corps, General Grubac, sends a request for the units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to take some features. In order for that to be done, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps has to receive an order from a person who is actually authorised to assign tasks and issue orders to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So could you tell me, why wasn't this sent to the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the Main Staff is on this address list. So I think that's a misstatement of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me just check properly. Yes, at least in the English translation, Mr. Petrusic, we do have the Main Staff of the army of the VRS anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Why was it not sent only to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading. That's the problem with leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is leading as well. I mean, he could easily rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it appears to me that this is not a leading question, because the question stems from it, and we don't have the answer to it in it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, the document speaks for itself. It indicates the addressees, okay? So if you - and we don't need the witness to confirm who the addressees were - so if you have a question arising out of that, put it, by all means. But otherwise, let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it might be a misunderstanding here. The question is not so much who is the addressee but rather why has this document not been solely sent to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let him -- let me rephrase it myself then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm sorry. Mr. Obradovic, if you look at this document you will see who the addressees are. In addition to the Main Staff, there is also the 2nd Krajina Corps and General Mladic personally. Why was it also sent to these last two; that is, the 2nd Krajina Corps and General Mladic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the Main Staff and the staff of the Main Staff should be notified about the developments, because we are following the developments in the whole theater, and we have to be told about this request by the Herzegovina Corps. The decision or the order to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps could only be issued by the commander. The commander of the Herzegovina Corps knows that General Mladic, his immediate superior, is at the command post of the 2nd Krajina Corps. And that is why it is sent to him, so that he could issue an order to the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And it is also sent to the Main Staff in order to enable us to monitor to developments. That would be my response, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an amendment to the transcript on page 36, line 16, it says here, "monitor developments," and the witness said, "prati situaciju."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which means what?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Follow the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to that -- this kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- nitpicking for argument's sake is what that appears to me to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but to Ms. Fauveau there is a difference between "follow the situation" and "monitor the developments." We can leave it at that and proceed. Come on. Your next question, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, do you have any knowledge whether the representatives of the command of the Main Staff have meetings with the civilian state leadership of the Republika Srpska, the government of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the representatives of the army were who took part in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, those were commanders and their assistants, but in some situations we would go there as a team. So not in an individual, but depending on what was being discussed by the government --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did General Milovanovic go to those meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you know whether in the absence of -- do you know whether in the absence of General Milovanovic, whether General Miletic did attend those meetings as an individual?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know any specific examples, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the -- any jurisdiction that UNPROFOR might have had in Republika Srpska in the territory that was controlled by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware of the details but I did note that they were peacekeepers; it was a peacekeeping force and they did have certain powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is whether you are on the same wavelength, you, Mr. Petrusic, and your witness, as to the extent of the meeting of -- meaning of "jurisdiction." If you could be more precise -- in other words, you were referring to other issues other than the ones that the witness referred to. You are free to put another question. I want to make sure that you were on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in the description of its tasks as the chief of the operations and training administration, did General Miletic also have this role to attend the sessions of the government of Republika Srpska and similar things?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In 1994 you joined the Main Staff, who received you at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Main Staff, the chief of the operations and training administration was not there. He was at the western front, and I was received by Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What did General Milovanovic offer you by way of a job, possible job?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did not make this offer immediately, but two or three days later. I accompanied General Milovanovic, General Tolimir, and Colonel Magazin, to Pale, to the meeting with the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR. I believe his name was Brickman, General Brickman. After that, General Milovanovic tasked me with processing this meeting, which I did; and he told me on that occasion that he thought since Colonel Magazin was about to retire to appoint me to his post. But he also told me that he had changed his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, but "processing a meeting." That has no meaning that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could also be a matter of translation, actually, but if you could clarify this with the witness, please. Perhaps you know better which words -- which terminology he used, and if that could be translated again, the same or differently we would be in a better position to know. Here we have: "After that, General Milovanovic tasked me with processing this meeting, which I did." Yes, Mr. Obradovic, let's come --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my task, Your Honour, when I say, "to process it," I had to write down how the meeting progressed and I had to write down the conclusions. And when I did that, when I handed this in to him, told me that he had thought that I would do this job; but then I changed his mind. I don't know for what reason. And then Lieutenant-Colonel Milo Djordjevic [as interpreted] was brought in to perform this job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So process in the sense of covering and reporting on. All right. Let's proceed. Mr. Petrusic, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Lieutenant-Colonel Milo Djordjevic, that's how it's recorded in the transcript; but can you tell us his name, his actual name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to those meetings with UNPROFOR. In the absence, to your knowledge, in the absence of General Miletic, General Milovanovic, the then-Colonel Miletic, did he attend those meetings with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any knowledge of that, but I do know that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the counsel please stop shuffling the papers, we cannot hear the witness from the noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Obradovic. You will need to repeat your -- sorry, one moment, Mr. Obradovic. You will need to repeat your answer because there was a problem that impeded the interpreters from hearing what you were saying. Mr. Petrusic, you are aware of what the interpreters complained of, so let's come back to you, Mr. Obradovic. What we have here is: "Well, I don't have any knowledge of that, but I do know that ..." can you continue from there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know that care was taken if a meeting was convened by the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff, then the chief of Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska attend the meeting. If it was the commander, then it was the commander who attended those meetings. Now, whether general or then-Colonel Miletic did attend those meetings, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the command of the Main Staff of the VRS, were there any morning briefings of the command held?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who attended those meetings in the command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the commander chaired the meeting, then the assistants were present there as well as the administration chiefs. If it was a meeting of the staff, then the officers -- the staff officers were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the administrations, what administration were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the independent administrations. The chief of administration for operations and training, which is not independent, because the chief of the -- this administration usually took notes, kept the minutes of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at document 5D1021.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we clarify the two independent entities. That's the second or third time he's made that reference; and I don't think it's clear who he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic -- or Mr. Obradovic, you can deal with it straight away. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The administration, well you use the term "entity." I didn't understand, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, when you were talking about morning briefings and when you are talking about independent administrations, when you are talking about assistant commanders, would you please allow us to go back to those issues, and could you please explain what independent administrations do you have in mind? I don't want to suggest anything to you. Just tell us in your own words what are independent administrations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were administrations for plan, development, and finances, and administrations for airforce and the entire airforce. There were also admissions which were not independent. The administration for security, the intelligence security, and the education security. The second one was in the Sector for Intelligence and Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And let's round this off. The two administrations, the one for the plan and finances and the one for airforce, who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were directly linked to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what about the other two?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were tied to the chief of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The other two administrations that you spoke about, the security administration and the administration for intelligence, who were they? Or, rather, what were they part of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two administrations were a part of the Sector for Intelligence and Security, and they are subordinated to the chief of that particular sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would that be the inner circle of the command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inner circle of the command consists of the assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the -- my learned friend is happy with this or whether he wants to explore the matter any further, whether he want us to go into the greater details of the structure? If not, let's move on to 5D1021. Could the Court please produce 5D1021.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is on the screen already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a document issued by the Main Staff on the 17th of July 1995, and it bears the signature of General Mladic. Could you please tell us -- I apologise, it is a block signature rather than the signature of General Ratko Mladic. Could you please tell us, first of all, whether this was the day when you returned to the Main Staff from sick leave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to the Main Staff on the 17th of July in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Look at the first and second paragraphs of this document, which is actually an order. My question is this: Your memory and this document, do they help you remember whether General Milovanovic was present on the 20th of July in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It transpires from this document that in addition to this festive part of the party, the commander orders the corps commanders to prepare a short debriefing or briefing on certain issues. And that will you will find in the second paragraph. This took place in Crna Rijeka, and General Milovanovic attended this debriefing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was anybody else present during the debriefing -- or, rather, do you remember any other people who attended?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the commander of the East Bosnian Corps was not there, but there was his Chief of Staff. As for the rest of the corps commanders, if memory serves me well, were present. And the debriefing was lead by the Chief of Staff, because the commander was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What functions of the Chief of Staff were -- and did General Miletic take them over in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic took over certain tasks within the staff during that period of time. The organisation of the work of the officers who remained there and who were not with General Milovanovic; for example, that was one of the duties that he had taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific and provide us with some more detail of that task?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was taken over was tied to the signing of the daily combat reports and the organisation of the work of the staff at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
