utterances.text: And what about the other functions of the Chief of Staff? Did the Chief of Staff transfer his other functions on to somebody?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, and there was no reason for that, for that matter. In the military we used to use a platitude, and we used to say, Wherever the commander is, that's the command post. Wherever the Chief of Staff is, that's where the place is, because both moveable and stationary communications means enabled people to communicate. Only a bad commander would not organise his communications to function from the position where he is at any given moment, so there were communications means that allowed us to communicate with the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was going to interrupt you, but you did not finish. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when it comes to the forward command posts, these can often be at the command posts of a subordinated unit for a corps command, for example. And that's when you use the infrastructure that already exists in the command post of the corps. So you would use their communication means as well. When this is not the case, however, pursuant to regulations, at a forward command post, one has to organise the same types of communications as one has at their normal command post. However, these communication means are on a somewhat smaller scale at a forward command post. What does this mean? You have to be able to communicate with your superior officer pursuant to the plan of the superior command. As for the subordinate commands, you should be able to communicate with them as well as with your basic command post. These are the communication lines that have to be established from the forward command post towards other command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did General Milovanovic establish such communication lines at the western front from October 1994? Could he communicate with the Main Staff, in other words?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was often in a position to communicate with the commander about the situation in that area in cases when General Milovanovic did not come back until a certain deadline to the forward command post. That communication line was protected by cryptographic protection; 63 was the type of the device that protected that communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, General Milovanovic also could communicate with the subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you have any knowledge about humanitarian convoys and about the passage of humanitarian convoys across the territories under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those convoys came from different directions, either from Belgrade, Zagreb, Sarajevo, it all depended on where they were sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In principle did the administration -- or, rather, strike that. Do you know who made decisions about the passage of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a rather huge area and a very vague question as for time. During the key periods of convoys, it's my understanding, this officer was not around. So I don't know what time-period he's talking about and what the relevance of 1993 might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take them one by one. Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you -- could you kindly remove your headphones, please. Mr. Petrusic, what's the relevance of 1993? Yes, but I don't want to answer the question myself. Speak in the microphone, to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, maybe I can help you. I think the question did not in any way relate to 1993. 1993, the witness, wasn't even serving at the Main Staff, so I can't quite see why the Prosecution refers to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was the point of my objection. I can't tell what he's talking -- what year he's talking about and what his knowledge is of these things from his position at the forward command post on the western front. There is just no foundation for these questions, and there is no time-period. So we can tighten it up, there may be no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you pinpoint exactly the time-period you are interested in and about which the witness could comfortably answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, I think we have to understand the procedure before we can make any comments and know whether there were any changes. We really need to understand what happened at the end of 1994 and the way procedures went in the Main Staff, because that is very close to the period that we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we can simplify it. The -- there was a first question to you, Mr. Obradovic, which you answered. The question was -- oh, I see. I will try to simplify matters for everyone. There was a first question to you, Mr. Obradovic, which was as follows: "General, sir, do you have any knowledge about humanitarian convoys and about the passage of humanitarian convoys across the territories under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?" And you, according to the transcript, answered as follows: "Those convoys came from different directions, either from Belgrade, Zagreb, Sarajevo, it all depended on where they were sent to." And then there was another question to which we don't have an answer as yet, and the question was as follows: "In principle, did the administration -- do you know, rather, who made decisions about the passage of humanitarian aid?" Now, I understand from what has been going on that you came into the picture - as far as passage of convoys are concerned - at a certain point in time. Let's starts from there. There was a time when you somehow was involved in this whole set up, or you were familiar with it. At that point in time are you aware as to who made the decisions about the passage of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the commander who made those decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can you tell us with some precision when you first started being involved in this area or when you became aware of how this area functioned? Was it in 1994, and if yes, what part of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediately at the outset, as soon as I joined the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we take it up from there now, Mr. Petrusic? You know what Mr. McCloskey's queries and concerns are; and you also heard Madam Fauveau explain what they were -- what you should be after. So let's proceed from there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have 5D884 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in the signature block of this document we can see General Nikolai. And on this document, do you see the handwritten initials? Can you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask the usher to give the witness the pen that he could use to write on the monitor, on the screen, so that he could circle the initials that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment General. On this document that you can see here on the right-hand side of your screen, could you please circle the two initials that you say you are able to recognise.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I circled?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you please mark it with number 1?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us whose initials are these?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's General Tolimir's initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you now please circle the other initials and could you please mark it with number 2?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Whose initials are those?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, in the initials you circled the Cyrillic letters where it says, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, above the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like the usher to give you another pen. General, wait a little bit, please. Things that are written in Cyrillic, where it says "da," "yes," could you please circle that, and could you put number 3.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So just to make things perfectly clear, the circle marked with 2 indicates the initials put there by General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Again, on this document, mid-way down the page, we can see the word, "da" written in Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, are you referring to the thing that I marked with number 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. And here the commander gives his approval to whoever is processing this document, and that is Colonel Djurdjic, indicating that this is approved and that he can start drafting the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mid-way down the page, again in Cyrillic alphabet, there is a note by Colonel Milos Djurdjic, can you please read that for us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, Captain Novakovic, the data about the movement urgently, this is underlined, report by phone to the checkpoints signed Colonel Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, the knowledge that you have from the administration, and you mentioned the person who processed this document, when we have this document, what is done with it in the department ran by Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may comment on what is written by hand in the upper part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up there, Captain Novakovic, that is my assumption, noted on this document that Caura was notified at 1135 hours, Domar was notified at 1138, and Bresa at 1140. Those are code names of units that Captain Novakovic was supposed to notify because of the urgency of the matter. He was supposed to phone them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, Colonel Milos Djurdjic, what department was he in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning, he was appoint the chief of the civil affairs department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who his superior was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This department was linked with the cabinet or office, in other words, he was under the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mean the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of the Main Staff. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We can remove this document. Could we please have document 846 -- oh, yes, before you remove it, could you please put today's date and your signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, he has. Mr. Obradovic, you have to sign it and date it, please. You can sign it either at the bottom or top, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the 13th today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No it's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the 14th today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I just get clarification on who he thinks wrote the Caura and the coded documents? That may save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Prosecutor did get the answer. He said it was -- the witness said it was Captain Novakovic and that was at page 51, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my clarification because I don't know where he got that from, and I thought he may have been meaning Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But it's clear, do you confirm that, Mr. Obradovic, so that we can proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's what I said. The order to Captain Novakovic by Colonel Djurdjic. So he stated here the times when he actually notified the units in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that we need this document anymore. Could we please have document 864 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 846.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D846. You can see on the first page that this was issued by the Main Staff on the 25th of November, 1994. On the second page of the document in the Serbian and English versions, we can see the signature block of General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or rather, that would be page 3, the last page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, please take some time and look at this document. Could you please tell us first, where did this document originate from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It originated from the Main Staff, the number designation 03/4. That's the designation of the operations and training administration, and it was drafted on the 25th of November of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At any rate, this is an order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your comment on this document in light of the fact that it originated from your administration?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. What's your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, what is the demand contained in this order from the commander of the Main Staff in accordance with this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent to the Drina Corps command, to the commander in person. And in the preamble, the commander of the Main Staff notifies the Drina Corps commander that he has approved the four UNPROFOR convoys, and that all four would pass on the 26th of November, 1994. And then, the routes are listed, the affiliation, the number of vehicles, and other data about the convoys. And before it says, "I hereby order ..." the commander of the Main Staff says: "Having assessed the overall situation, the relations with UNPROFOR, and the decision of the Main Staff ..." to effect a blockade of four convoys. And in order to implement the said decision, he now specifies in 7 items the assessment, the organisation, the procedure when convoys are stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us what are the reasons why the four convoys are stopped and why those searches are carried out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were cases when illicit goods were being transported or when goods that were not declared and equipment that was not declared was being transported. In some cases, it was even ammunition that was being carried. There probably was some suspicion since this long blockade is envisaged for the search to be carried out, and in item 5 he prohibits any arbitrary or disorganised behaviour on part of our troops that participate in the implementation of this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to move to the next document. We are not going to need this anymore. And that would be 5D1311. It's a document from the Main Staff. The date is the 6th of March, 1995. In the English version, let us move on to page 3. And in the Serbian version, could you please just scroll down the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, at the end of the document in the Serbian version, you can see the signature block standing in for the Chief of Staff Colonel Radivoje Miletic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Below the signature block, there is a signature in ink. Do you know whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel Pandzic, Radoslav Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like the usher to provide the witness with a pen so that you could circle the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we clarify whether there is a "za" in front of that signature or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can answer that question straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is a little bit not clear, but I believe that below the stamp you can see something. I think I can discern the outline of the letter Z there, or maybe that's number 8. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we zoom in that part first before the witness makes any markings. Further, could we zoom in further, and further. Can we concentrate on the left part only, put it close to the centre; and zoom further, please. Does that help you any better, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it looks like a Z, letter Z, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the second mobile that we've heard today. One had jingle bells, this one is ... it's good judges have got the gift of patience. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we won't need the signature to be circled, and I apologise to Madam Usher in light of the fact that the General was able to identify the signature as that of Colonel Pandzic. Could we please have both documents on the screen. Could you now go to the next page in both documents. The English version too, please. Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you see the initials that are outside of the circle where it says "A/A" in Cyrillic. Could you please tell us whose initials are those?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the initials of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please leaf through this document. It contains eight more pages. Have you gone through all of them? Could you please tell us then whose initials are there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the initials of the commander of the Main Staff, lieutenant-general -- or, rather, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What does he want to do with his initials?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he read -- well, Your Honours, if you'll allow me to explain the procedure. The facts from the civil affairs department is on at all times, and these requests come in through that fax machine. And then Colonel Djurdjic takes them to the commander for his information, and then the commander reads all of them, and he underlines things; and then he either approves them or he puts them -- he instructs them that they should be put in the files, A/A or put some restrictions. For instance, here he says, No fuel; and then Colonel Djurdjic uses this as a basis for his own document that he's going to draft. Because every number that is listed in the memo written -- signed by Colonel Pandzic contains the numerical designation of each convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break, are you saying that the signature, General Mladic's signature is in fact an order tantamount to an order to Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection, yes. I don't think that needs a follow-up by way of explanation. Could you rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic, is he duty-bound to comply with the instructions that are given in this fax by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We had the rules on office work a little while ago, and it gives powers to the commander to give instructions to whoever is processing the documents on the margin. And these are, in fact, notifications of convoy passage and instructions what to do about them. This was just one document, two documents in one. And since General Miletic was away standing in for the Chief of Staff, this was signed by Colonel Pandzic from the airforce and air defence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to suggest what we have our break now, and we will go back to this document after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We will have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can set aside this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I would now like to ask you once again to slow down and to make pauses before answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move on to document 5D1312. In the English version you can see the heading. Could you please put the English version on page 7, and in the Serbian version that would be page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in both versions the signature block reads as follows: "Stands in for the Chief of Staff, Colonel Radivoje Miletic." Could you please look at the document that you have in front of you, the one in Serbian; whose signature is it, the signature in ink?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pandzic, Radoslav Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like the -- for some technical assistance, could we please zoom in the part where the signature is affixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just -- sorry, it's not working. Okay. Just we can see from the English translation, it says, "Deputy chief of staff." That may be a translation issue. We will sort that out and get back to you on that to determine whether that's standing in or that -- and make sure we get that done correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of Colonel Pandzic, and do you see just before the area where the stamp is, is there anything handwritten there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says, "for [Realtime transcript read in error, "4"]" and the signature is that of Colonel Radoslav Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the person listed in the signature block is Colonel Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to speak into the microphone. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 59, line 12, instead of the figure "4" should read "for," F-O-R.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please leaf through the attachments to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put page 1 on the screen -- or, rather, page 8 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Have you gone through the document, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose initials are affixed to these documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those documents bear the initials of the commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the front page of this document, in the Serbian version, we see an instruction written in Cyrillic. Could you please read it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right-hand side it is written in Cyrillic, yes, and then it is stricken through.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No, no. General, on the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the typed-up document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hand over only to the Drina Corps because I faxed it to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Colonel Djurdjic. This is notification to the encryption operator that he needn't send an encrypted version of this document to the Sarajevo Corps because it had already been faxed. The only encrypted version is to be sent to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: For the record, this note that you talked about, who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the encryption operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the chain of command of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, did Colonel, later General Miletic allow to issue orders to Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not part of the same chain of command. In fact, Colonel Djurdjic was subordinated directly to the office of the commander or the person of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 17th of July, the day when you returned to the Main Staff. Upon your return whom did you find there, and could you please describe briefly your return to the staff of the Main Staff or to your office?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I travelled in my own car. The driver was a retired police officer from Bosanski Brod, and Colonel [as interpreted] Dragan Micanovic was a passenger. Upon my arrival I reported to the chief of the administration, and I told him -- I asked him what was happening, and he told me about that. And there were very few people there the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It is Lieutenant Dragan Micanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who was the other passenger?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dragan Micanovic, a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information as to what was going on? Were you briefed about what was going on in the area of the army of Republika Srpska in that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Lieutenant Micanovic we received information in the course of our trip, that from Zvornik to Hans Pijesak we should be careful because we might encounter armed groups of BH army troops from Srebrenica. Upon our arrival in the Main Staff, I learned that there were problems in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps around Vlasic, the East Bosnian Corps up there at Majevica, the Stolice repeater, in the Drina Corps where there was combat ongoing for the Zepa area. In the Sarajevo Romanija Corps area, there was a critical situation to the south and northwest of the area. And in Herzegovina Corps, the situation was difficult in Treskavica and in the area towards Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us now dwell on the Drina Corps. Did you know, were you aware, who was engaged in combat around Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drina Corps was engaged in combat in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the involvement of the Main Staff in the planning and execution of combat, first planning then execution?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well the combat operations were not planned at the level of the Main Staff. The combat operations were planned by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, given that we know that the operation started on the 14th of July, 1995, and you returned on the 17th, how did you know that the operations were not planned at the level of the Main Staff? Just a moment, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the obligation of the operations department and the operations and training administration to follow the combat operations in the whole theatre, operations that are planned at the level of the Main Staff are plotted on the work map of the Main Staff. We did not have any details about the combat operations in Zepa, and we didn't have any written orders in the form of an order in order to be able to follow that more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: There is evidence to the effect that General Mladic was in that part of the theater as was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an area in the Zepa sector. The name is Pribicevac. This was a forward command post of the Drina Corps for combat operations in the territory of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We also have information that -- that Pribicevac was not a forward command post of the Drina Corps for Zepa operations -- just a moment, but that it was rather a forward command post for a different operation. I would just like to make sure that you did not misspeak.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did misspeak. It was a Boksanica, they were at that area of Zepa, called Boksanica, I believe. I am not sure though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: While you were at the Main Staff, General Miletic was there every day, was he not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was at the time and could you, yourself, take a look at the operation around Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not have anything to do with the Zepa operation. He was involved in current things at the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports from the Zepa theater?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular combat reports arrived from the Drina Corps because that was the area of their responsibility, and these reports also contained information about the developments around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who was the one who drafted those combat reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those to the Supreme Commander, it was General Miletic, myself, or possibly Krsto Djeric's, if he was there. And as for the corps command, I really don't know who drafted the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you find Colonel Trkulja there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I arrived, together with Micanovic, I inquired about Colonel Trkulja because he was deployed together with us and he also belonged to the staff. I asked, Where is Trki? That was his nickname. General Miletic told me that he had sent him together with some other officers to the area of the Zvornik Brigade upon the order of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what about General Milovanovic, was he there at the General Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th, no he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer the previous question and tell us what General Miletic told you about Colonel Trkulja upon your arrival in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had sent him together with some other officers of the Main Staff upon the order of the commander of the Main Staff to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like the Court to produce 5D1205. If this could be placed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this document is about reporting. Or, let me put it this way. Do you know the definition of the staff units at the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the deployment of the Main Staff, there was the 67th signals regiment and the 65th protection motorised regiment. The 1st guards brigade was resubordinated to the command of the Herzegovina Corps, and it was deployed in Karnovink [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The combat reports that are mentioned in this document, why were they sent to Colonel Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the area was very small and it contained both the command of the signals regiment command and the motorised regiment command, in order to avoid confusing the code, I believe, this was the order of the chief of the General Staff that the chiefs of the staffs of these two units should report to Colonel Miletic and to brief him instead of writing daily reports. And this document here, signed by Savcic, the commander of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment regulates this issue. And I believe that he had previously received this order either in writing or orally from the commander [as interpreted] of the staff. I wouldn't be able to tell you what kind of order it was. It says here that Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic would be in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we better clear up some of the those titles. We got it translated as the commander of the staff, and I don't think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is everyone in agreement with that, particularly you, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "chief of staff," I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, let's proceed then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It says in this document that it is issued by Major Savcic based on a verbal order by the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was that common practice in 1995 when you were --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: -- in the staff? Tell me, please, what is the basis of regular and interim combat reports? How are they drafted, based on what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common practice and obligation on the part of the subordinated units to report on the developments and the course of combat activities. Regular combat reports are drafted once a day, interim as needed. And sometimes unified or combination reports are written at higher level units, when combat takes longer and one report follows at the end of those combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To what extent is a combat report important for the superior command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to military rules, a lot of emphasis is put on reporting. It has to be timely and correct or accurate. Why is that? This is in order for the commander to be able to correct his decision with respect to the original decision in keeping with the development of situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce P207 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number. Due to the background noise, the interpreter is afraid that she did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D1007.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, take your time, look at this document. General, sir, are you familiar with the -- with situations of the kind described by the Chief of Staff Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document issued by the Main Staff, dated 4 June 1993, by which chief of the general staff, Manojlo Milovanovic, warns all corps commands VNPBO, as well as the staff brigades about the weaknesses that have been noticed in daily combat reporting, about some inaccuracies and the low usage value of these reports. And after this clause: "I order ..." he says, and I quote that: "Combat reports should be sent daily in accordance with the time as regulated before." And it also says that: "Before combat reports are sent they must be checked and signed by the commander." And only in his absence by the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following document is 5D1010. This is another document by Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly, please, whether in 1994 the practice persists and that poor reporting continues and the poor usage or value of regular or combat reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is confirmed by the document which was drafted for that very reason. I -- the super command cannot make decisions based on a poor and inaccurate combat reports that they receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What was the basis of the knowledge that the reports were inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different situations. There are even some trivial situations. It was common practice for the commander of the Main Staff, everyday, 2000 hours, to talk to the corps commanders, airforce, the PVO, and the centre of military schools. In those immediate contacts, the corps commander would, for example, ask his commander for a leave to visit his family or deal with a private business; whereas, in the combat report of that same unit, it says that the commander went to inspect his units. And it turned out that this was not correct. There were some intentional omissions of certain events or developments for various reasons. For example, the corps commander did not dare communicate bad news to the commander of the Main Staff, and an example of that was when I met Lieutenant Bora Djordjevic, who worked in the Main Staff press centre. He hailed from Blatnica which is south of the town of Teslic. And since I had spent some time in that area before joining the Main Staff, I asked him about his family and his area down there. He says, I just came back yesterday. Everything has fallen, Djokic [phoen] to Perici. And then I said, Well, it's nonsense. I read the report of the 1st Krajina Corps and there is no reference to such a bad situation at all. As we shook hands, I reported to my superior, the chief of administration, General Miletic, then he went to the Chief of Staff; and then they called me to convey the message to the Chief of Staff, so to speak, from the horse's mouth as I heard it, myself. And then they called General Tolimir as well. And then he went down the security line and called Colonel Stevo Bogojevic and asked him whether the information that he had actually received was actually true. The latter confirmed that, and when General Tolimir asked him to write a report, he said, Well, I can't. My commander wouldn't allow me to write a report of that sort. This is, for example, one way of information reaching superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P37. You've already spoken about that document before. Can the document be scrolled down, please, to the signature block. It should be on the following page in the English version. And the Serbian version can be moved to the beginning of the page or the beginning of the document. Since the document contains just one page in the Serbian, we need the beginning of that first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You've already spoken about this situation, General, could you please look at number 03/4-1670 in the heading of this document. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What administration is this? Whose number is this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 03/4-1670, this is the administration for training and operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would this be an order that belongs to the group of combat documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Which documents were originated from this administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders relative to the activities of the administration for training and operations. Orders are issued in other organs and pertain to their respective activities but they are signed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And you are saying that this is obviously an order by Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who has given the administration for training and operations elements for composing this order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the order giver or order issuer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to some foundation. I mean, this is his first day back. Can we get foundation on how he is answering these questions? Is it just by reading the document or something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he needs to explain that. Mr. Obradovic, on what basis are you in a position or you feel you are in a position to give the answers that you have been giving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my subsequent information about these events provide me with the right to speak the way I do. When I arrived, it was said because of an unclear situation in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, it was ordered for Trkulja with a group officers to go there to the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that still does not tell us anything about his relationship to this document. In fact, his answer is somewhat concerning because it says, "My subsequent information."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way I understood him was precisely that he thinks he's in a position to answer questions on this document based on the information he gained later on, not at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I knew that Colonel Trkulja had gone there. I didn't know at the time what other officers were with him. Because my arrival and contact with the chief of the administration was to learn about Trkulja. That was my specific question. And then he told me that he was sent upon the order of the commander of the Main Staff to the Zvornik Brigade because the situation was rather unclear there. This is my recollection and then the information that I received on the 17th at the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's clear. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, because there are so many documents coming, I think it's incumbent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are still halfway through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's incumbent upon counsel to at least determine whether this person drafted this document, whether he's seen it, before he starts commenting on it. As a pure matter of foundation, I understand what he's saying, and I have no problem with it. He's said it a long time ago, but we still don't know how he relates to this document and before he starts talking about it foundationally, he must in an ordered system, at least tell us if he's authored it or seen it or he knows anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I -- we can order Mr. Petrusic to put that question, unless he thinks it will speed up things and he can get an answer. Otherwise, you deal with it on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My foundation for the question was the nature of the documents, i.e., whether they are normally generated in the administration for training and operations, and whether the number of this administration is 03/4. That was the foundation for my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then I asked who it was in that administration who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And furthermore who is it in the administration who drafts orders. That was my question to the witness, and I'm still waiting for his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the administration for training and operations, the orders are drafted by the chief of administration, and I, as the chief of department, but I did not draft this because the document was drafted on the 17th, on the day when I was still on the way. And the person that I inquired about had already been sent out on a mission. And the document probably was not -- not in the administration itself. It must have been sent for coding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My next question would be this: Who in the administration provided you with elements to allow you to issue your orders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the commander, sometimes the Chief of Staff, after their conversation. They would give us their starting points and elements for any orders; and based on such conclusions, we would draft our orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Unless we are -- you have one final question on this subject matter, I think we need to finish here and continue Monday because in less than 30 minutes, I have another sitting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and it may be translation issue, but I doubt this man said that he was issuing orders and that's what the -- when they were very quickly going through this, that's what we end up seeing on the translation, so it may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- need clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You will see to it between now and Monday, and we will clarify it on Monday. Just to have an indication of, especially for your colleagues for planning purposes, Mr. Petrusic, how much more time do you think you will require? This is inconvenient speaking to a column, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will be able to stick to my original time, or maybe a bit longer, maybe a bit over four-and-a-half hours; but I believe I won't be able to finish before the end of the first session. It will probably go over into the second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So the next in line, Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Ostojic, you have advance notice on that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is unlikely that I will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A half hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I did this exercise so that you and others will be prepared knowing that you will be cross-examining the witness Monday. We stand adjourned until Monday. Same advisory, Mr. Obradovic, as yesterday, you are not to discuss this with anyone or let anyone talk to you about these issues. Okay? Thank you. Have a nice weekend, all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
